items.foco: Most common viral cause: Coxsackie B
items.title: Predominant viral etiology
items.contentHtml:
Most common viral cause

  • Coxsackie B (enterovirus) is the most common viral cause of acute myocarditis in endemic areas.
  • Other viruses: parvovirus B19 (currently more detected in biopsies in Europe), adenovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus.
  • Mechanism: direct myocyte damage by viral cytolysis and immune response mediated by cytotoxic T lymphocytes.
  • Etiological diagnosis is supported by paired serology (IgM and IgG) and polymerase chain reaction in blood or biopsy.
  • Examination trap: in children and young adults, Coxsackie B is classic; but in current biopsies, parvovirus B19 is the most prevalent.

items.foco: Triad: chest pain, fever, heart failure
items.title: Typical clinical presentation
items.contentHtml:
Classic triad

  • The triad of chest pain, fever and heart failure (HF) is suggestive, but not always complete; HF can be subclinical.
  • Chest pain: pleuritic or ischemic type, often preceded by viral syndrome (fever, myalgia, fatigue) 1-2 weeks before.
  • Fever: present in the acute phase, helps differentiate from acute myocardial infarction (AMI) without ST elevation.
  • HF: dyspnea, orthopnea, edema; It can debut as cardiogenic shock in fulminant myocarditis.
  • In young people with chest pain and elevated troponin, always consider acute myocarditis as a differential diagnosis of acute coronary syndrome.

items.foco: Diffuse ST elevation and PR depression
items.title: Characteristic electrocardiogram
items.contentHtml:
ECG in acute myocarditis

  • Key finding: diffuse elevation of the ST segment (concave upward) in multiple leads, without mirror image typical of infarction.
  • Depression of the PR segment (especially in leads II, V5-V6) is an early and specific sign, associated with accompanying pericarditis.
  • Other alterations: tachycardia sinus, first degree atrioventricular block, inverted T waves, low voltage QRS if pericardial effusion.
  • Differentiate from acute myocardial infarction with ST elevation (STEMI): diffuse elevation without reciprocal changes and depression of the PR point to myocarditis/pericarditis.
  • ST elevation is usually >1 mm in two contiguous leads, but It does not follow coronary distribution.

items.foco: Elevated troponin with normal coronary arteries
items.title: Biomarkers and angiography
items.contentHtml:
Troponin and coronary arteries

  • The troponin (TnI or TnT) is elevated in most cases, reflecting non-ischemic myocardial damage.
  • The elevation of troponin is sensitive but not specific; its kinetics are prolonged and do not follow the typical pattern of infarction.
  • Coronary angiography shows normal coronary arteries (absence of significant stenosis), which supports the diagnosis in a clinical context.
  • Coronary angiography is indicated in adults with suspected acute coronary syndrome to rule out atherosclerotic disease.
  • The relationship between elevated troponin and ventricular dysfunction without coronary obstruction should raise suspicion. myocarditis, takotsubo or coronary embolism.

items.title: Gold standard diagnosis
items.contentHtml:
Endomyocardial biopsy

  • The endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) is the definitive diagnosis (gold standard) of acute myocarditis, although its sensitivity is limited by sampling.
  • Main indications: hemodynamic deterioration, failure to respond to empirical treatment, suspicion of specific etiology (sarcoidosis, eosinophilic, giants).
  • It is typically obtained from the right interventricular septum guided by fluoroscopy or echocardiography; ≥5 samples are recommended to increase performance.
  • Complications: cardiac perforation, tamponade, arrhythmias, valvular injury (low risk <1% in expert centers).
  • Examination trap: not necessary in all cases; In mild and stable myocarditis, the diagnosis is based on clinical symptoms, biomarkers, electrocardiogram (ECG) and magnetic resonance imaging.

items.title: Histological classification
items.contentHtml:
Dallas Criteria

  • The Dallas Criteria define active myocarditis as myocardial inflammatory infiltrate with necrosis or non-ischemic degeneration of adjacent myocytes.
  • Borderline myocarditis (borderline): scant or focal inflammatory infiltrate without necrosis, requires clinical correlation.
  • Myocarditis chronic: fibrosis with persistent inflammatory infiltrate, without active necrosis.
  • The absence of infiltrate and necrosis is reported as negative for myocarditis (sensitivity limited by sampling error).
  • The Dallas Criteria have high specificity but low sensitivity; They are complemented by immunohistochemistry (lymphocytes >14 cells/mm²) and viral polymerase chain reaction.

items.foco: Classic in young people after viral infection
items.title: Epidemiology and context
items.contentHtml:
Affected population

  • Acute myocarditis is classic in young people (adults <40 years) and in children, after a respiratory or gastrointestinal viral infection.
  • The peak incidence occurs in young men (ratio 2:1) and in spring/summer due to enterovirus.
  • The presentation can be similar to a coronary syndrome. acute with chest pain and elevated troponin, but with normal coronary arteries on angiography.
  • Sudden death is a feared complication, especially in athletes; Therefore exercise restriction is recommended.
  • Complete recovery occurs in the majority (60-70%), but it can progress to chronic dilated cardiomyopathy.

items.foco: Echocardiogram: ventricular dysfunction and pericardial effusion
items.title: Echocardiographic findings
items.contentHtml:
Echocardiogram in myocarditis

  • The transthoracic echocardiogram is the first imaging test; may show ventricular dysfunction (global or segmental, often non-coronary) and pericardial effusion.
  • Ventricular function may be normal in mild forms; the presence of effusion supports pericardial involvement (myopericarditis).
  • Other findings: increased wall thickness due to edema (hyperechogenic myocardium), chamber dilation, regional motility disorders.
  • The echocardiogram also evaluates complications: intracavitary thrombus, mitral regurgitation, diastolic dysfunction.
  • The left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <40% is a poor prognostic factor; It is used to decide treatment and follow-up.

items.title: Diagnostic cardioresonance
items.contentHtml:
Cardiac magnetic resonance

  • Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) is the non-invasive technique of choice for diagnosis and follow-up.
  • Key finding: subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement (patchy or diffuse pattern), which spares the subendocardium (unlike infarction).
  • Other Lake Louise criteria: myocardial edema in sequences T2 (increased signal), hyperemia (early enhancement) and fibrosis with late enhancement.
  • CMR has high sensitivity and specificity (~80-90%) for acute myocarditis; It is recommended to perform it within 2 weeks of onset.
  • The subepicardial distribution of enhancement is associated with viral etiology; mesocardial enhancement may be seen in sarcoidosis.

items.foco: Complication: fulminant myocarditis and sudden death
items.title: Serious complications
items.contentHtml:
Fulminant myocarditis and sudden death

  • Fulminant myocarditis presents with acute onset, cardiogenic shock and the need for inotropic or mechanical circulatory support.
  • sudden death may be the first manifestation, especially in young athletes; causes ventricular arrhythmias and complete atrioventricular block.
  • Risk factors for poor prognosis: low cardiac output, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <35%, wide QRS complexes, giant cell etiology.
  • Treatment of fulminant includes balloon pump support, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), or ventricular assist.
  • Recovery of fulminant myocarditis can be complete if the acute phase is overcome, unlike the chronic phase.

items.foco: Treatment: support, avoid NSAIDs and steroids
items.title: Therapeutic management
items.contentHtml:
Treatment of myocarditis

  • Treatment is mainly support: rest, monitoring, management of heart failure (HF) with diuretics, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE inhibitors) or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) and beta-blockers.
  • Avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) in the acute phase because they can increase damage myocardial disease and mortality in animal models.
  • Corticosteroids (steroids) are not routinely used; They are indicated in specific cases: giant cell myocarditis, eosinophilic, sarcoidosis, lupus or associated with immunotherapy toxicity.
  • In viral myocarditis, antivirals have no proven benefit; intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) is reserved for children or severe cases, without solid evidence.
  • Circulatory support (inotropes, ECMO) is used in refractory shock; Heart transplant is the last option in patients who do not recover ventricular function.

items.foco: Restriction of physical exercise for 3-6 months
items.title: Activity recommendations
items.contentHtml:
Exercise restriction

  • Physical exercise restriction for 3-6 months is recommended in all patients with acute myocarditis, even if ventricular function is normal.
  • Restriction includes avoidance of competitive sports and intense exercise; rest reduces the risk of arrhythmias and progression of inflammatory damage.
  • Before resuming activity, evaluation with echocardiogram, electrocardiogram (ECG) and Holter monitoring for arrhythmias should be performed.
  • Low-level exercise (walking) is allowed after the acute phase, but return to full training is decided individually.
  • In athletes who have had myocarditis, complete resolution of inflammation (evidence by MRI) and absence of inducible arrhythmias are required before passing the competition.
